journal.description: One row per journal. This is the main/master journal table — the source of truth for a journal's identity, access type, publication/lifecycle status, identifiers, and descriptive/marketing information. The primary key for joins is journal_id. For journal identification: use title when the user provides or asks for the journal's full name; use jms_jcode when the user refers to a journal by its short code/abbreviation such as CMC, COC, CDR, CPD, CP, etc. For subscription vs Open Access questions, use jtype (O = Open Access, S = Subscription). This table does not by itself contain who the actual editors are or what roles they hold; those assignments live in tbl_ebm, reachable via the join below.

joins.note: This join connects a journal to its actual editorial board: it lets you find every editor and every role assigned to a given journal (via tbl_ebm), which this table alone cannot answer.

tbl_ebm.description: One row represents one editor holding one editorial role for one journal. This is the central relationship/junction table connecting journals, editors, and editorial roles — most questions that combine any two of 'which journal', 'which person', and 'which role' need this table as the hub. Use journal_id to join to journal.journal_id. Use editor_id to join to tbl_editors.editor_id for editor/person details. Use ebm_role_id to join to tbl_ebm_role.role_id for role identification. This table also carries assignment-level details such as main_section, section, region, acceptance_date, resign_date, approval status, and ebm_status. ebm_status describes the status of THIS specific editor-role-journal assignment and is a separate concept from tbl_editors.status (the editor's own account status). For current/active assignments, normally filter ebm_status = 'Active' unless the user explicitly asks about resigned, historical, or inactive assignments.

joins.note: This join gives you the journal's identity and attributes for an editorial assignment — its title, jms_jcode, jtype (Open Access/Subscription), and other journal-level fields — none of which live on tbl_ebm itself.
This join gives you the actual person behind an assignment — their name, degree, institute/university, country, and other profile fields — none of which live on tbl_ebm itself.
This join gives you the real, current role name (role and nicename) for an assignment — resolve the role through this join.

tbl_ebm_role.description: One row per defined editorial role. This is a role lookup/reference table — it defines what each role MEANS, but does not by itself say who holds it or for which journal. The primary key is role_id. Use role_id to join tbl_ebm.ebm_role_id to this table whenever the user asks about an editorial role such as EIC, Co-EIC, Regional Editor, Section Editor, or another role. role holds the shorter/original form of the role name; nicename holds the fuller, more readable form. Match against whichever of the two more closely resembles the user's own wording.

joins.note: This join gives you every actual assignment that uses this role — which editor holds it and on which journal — which this table cannot answer on its own.

tbl_editors.description: One row per editor/person. This table holds an editor's identity and profile information — name, academic degree, professional title, university/institute/department, area of expertise, country, contact details, and researcher identifiers such as ORCID, Scopus ID, and ResearcherID. The primary key is editor_id. This table does not by itself say which journal an editor works for or what role they hold — those relationships live in tbl_ebm, reachable via the join below. The status column here describes the person's own account status (A = Active, B = Blocked, D = Deleted) and is a separate concept from tbl_ebm.ebm_status, which describes the status of one specific journal-role assignment.

joins.note: This join gives you every journal and role assignment this editor actually holds — which this table cannot answer on its own.
